title: Combat System
summary: Specifies the real-time third-person combat model, four-character party, swapping, actions, resources, targeting, statuses, readability and encounter logic.

blocks.text: Editorial note. The historical source for this document still contains several turn-based terms. The current project direction is a real-time third-person Action RPG. This English edition preserves the underlying design intent while normalizing legacy references to the current real-time combat model. Party swapping and several defensive inputs remain subject to prototype validation.

Combat in Symphony of Justice should be engaging because it asks the player to understand the characters, read situations, and build meaningful relationships between abilities rather than simply selecting the action that produces the largest number.

The project documentation already establishes that profession, element, and personal talent can create synergies, and that those interactions should extend beyond raw damage increases. The Game Vision reinforces this principle by treating characters, elements, professions, talents, and relationships as meaningful inputs into team construction.
The strategic fantasy should revolve around three questions:
What is the enemy trying to do?
What tools does my party have to answer it?
In what sequence should I use those tools to create the outcome I want?
Combat should make the following decisions matter:
which character should be active at a given moment;
which enemy or enemy part represents the current priority;
when to spend or preserve resources;
when to apply an element or status;
when to trigger or exploit an interaction;
when to attack, protect, heal, reposition, or prepare;
how to adapt a party to different encounters;
when to accept risk in exchange for a greater reward.
The intended satisfaction comes from creating a sequence with purpose:

Excessive automation. Historical design explored automated offensive, defensive, and utility behaviors. Those ideas may remain as legacy reference, but automation should never replace the player's main combat decisions.
Universal rotations. A single fixed sequence of abilities should not solve nearly every encounter.
Trivial combinations. An elemental reaction should not automatically be correct simply because two elements can interact.
Statistics above strategy. A party with higher power should not completely invalidate mechanical understanding.
Power creep as the primary content model. New characters should open new possibilities before they simply replace older ones.
Enemies as health sponges. Increasing HP and damage should not be the only way to increase difficulty.
Combat in Symphony of Justice should reward planning, adaptation, execution, and understanding of the relationships between characters.
The proposed exploration and combat party consists of:
Four characters provide enough room for different functions and synergies without making the encounter state unnecessarily difficult to read.
specialized compositions built around a profession, element, reaction, or unique mechanic.
The system should not force a single universal party template.

Current real-time direction: one party member is directly controlled at a time, while the player can access the rest of the four-character party through quick swapping. This approach is PROPOSED and must be validated in the combat prototype.
changing the full party composition outside combat;
quickly swapping the active character during normal combat if the prototype validates the feature;
character-specific assist, substitution, or follow-up mechanics where they reinforce individual kit identity;
special modes that may later support reserves or additional party rules.

The goal is to make swapping a strategic tool rather than an input the player presses mechanically on cooldown. If universal swapping does not improve readability or combat feel during prototyping, the exact implementation can be revised.
The historical documentation establishes three fundamental kit actions:
The real-time combat model expands this foundation with movement, dodge, targeting, and party swapping while preserving the identity of each character's core kit.
The Basic Attack is the character's always-available offensive action.
generates a small amount of Ultimate Energy or character-specific resources;
may have character-specific variants or combo chains.
Historical material also references variants of the physical attack. These can be reinterpreted as:
Basic Attack. The conventional attack sequence.
Enhanced Basic Attack. A modified version unlocked by a talent, state, resource, stance, or specific condition.
Not every character needs an enhanced form.
Each character has a compact set of abilities tied to:

Skills primarily use cooldowns and may also consume or generate character-specific resources. A distinctive character mechanic can modify how a Skill behaves or cause one input to produce different effects under different conditions.
A reasonable prototype baseline is one primary active Skill per character, with a second Skill or alternate state only when it is essential to that character's identity.
The player should constantly weigh whether to use an ability immediately or preserve it for a better timing window.
The Ultimate is the strongest expression of a character's kit.
Each Ultimate should feel specific to the character rather than a generic high-damage button. The current proposal uses Ultimate Energy generated through combat actions.
Separating Ultimate Energy from normal cooldowns creates a second pacing layer: basic actions and Skills establish momentum, while the Ultimate represents a deliberate payoff.
Dodge is a core real-time defensive verb. Enemy telegraphs should allow the player to identify dangerous attacks, move or dodge, and punish the resulting recovery window.

A universal Guard input is not yet locked. Guard may exist as a prototype feature, a weapon-specific action, or a kit-specific mechanic for defensive characters. When used, it can reduce incoming damage and create a defensive advantage such as a counterattack, disarm, shield, or improved follow-up.
Defensive actions are most useful when:
an enemy prepares a dangerous telegraphed attack;
the player needs to survive while waiting for a cooldown or opening;
a tank or Guardian converts defense into protection, Taunt, a shield, or a counter.
Items may be available in normal PvE content, including:
Historical documentation already includes food and other consumables that modify statistics or support character functions.

Bosses, competitive modes, and post-game combat may restrict or disable item usage. Cooperative activities may allow selected consumables to support teamwork, but their exact rules belong to later balancing and mode-specific documentation.
MOVE | DODGE | ATTACK | SKILL | ULTIMATE | SWAP | ITEM
The surface should be easy to understand. The depth comes from timing, interactions, positioning, and character identity.
The project supports a hybrid resource model: HP and Ultimate Energy create a shared combat language, while unique resources allow individual characters to break or reinterpret those common rules.
HP represents a character's ability to remain in combat.
This principle is inherited directly from the historical design.
Ultimate Energy is a separate resource used to activate Ultimate abilities.
taking damage for characters or tank roles designed around that interaction;
Generation rates can differ by character. The historical Energy Recharge statistic can be reinterpreted as a modifier to this generation.
One of the strongest opportunities in the combat system is that not every character needs to obey exactly the same resource rules.
Juro. His abilities can consume HP, while his kit progressively generates tentacles up to a documented maximum of eight.
Future characters may use resources such as:
HP and Ultimate Energy form the common language; unique resources create character identity.
The player should be able to make meaningful targeting decisions without turning real-time combat into slow menu navigation.

The current Action RPG direction should support spatial targeting through camera orientation, soft targeting, aim assistance, or lock-on where appropriate. Exact behavior must be tested for controller and keyboard/mouse.
Ability shapes can still be classified using familiar targeting patterns:
Special encounters may include selectable or damageable enemy parts. Historical documentation already contemplated bosses with weak points or priority components.

Historical documentation includes Provocation as a statistic associated with the probability of receiving enemy attacks. In the real-time model, this can become a readable Threat / Taunt Weight system rather than a purely random value.
AI threat values influence target selection;
explicit Taunt abilities strongly increase or temporarily force enemy priority;
enemy-specific rules can override normal threat behavior when telegraphed clearly.
Juro already has a conceptual chain ability that increases his threat and redirects damage toward him, providing a useful precedent.
Guardian-style characters may protect allies by:
protecting allies within a defined area or range;
reacting to enemy attacks with counters or defensive follow-ups.
Status effects should be grouped into clear families and communicated consistently.
The documentation already includes characters such as Suki whose identity is tied to strengthening or exploiting debuffs.
Stun: temporarily interrupts or prevents actions;
Freeze: temporarily immobilizes or applies a special frozen condition;
Silence: limits selected abilities or categories of abilities;
Root: prevents movement while allowing other actions where appropriate;
Slow / Delay: reduces movement, action tempo, or the timing of specific mechanics.
The strongest control effects should have resistance, reduced duration, diminishing returns, or encounter-specific limits against bosses.

The project already contains mechanics based on sustained damage. Seals, for example, have historically been described as a source of continuous damage, while Yuzuki has concepts linked to damage-over-time bonuses.
Healing restores HP. Shields absorb damage before HP is reduced.
Hizuka provides a strong documented precedent: her Medical profession increases healing and converts part of that healing into shielding.
Cleanse is not fully defined in the historical documentation and should therefore remain PROPOSED rather than CANON.
convert negative states into benefits in specialized kits.
Not every support character should have access to Cleanse.
Every status should communicate: WHAT IT DOES | DURATION | STACKS | SOURCE
All mandatory enemies or encounter objectives are resolved.
Special encounters may use alternative objectives such as:
escape or reach an extraction point.
The default defeat condition is reached when the full active party can no longer continue.
Special encounters may also fail because of:
the character can no longer be directly controlled;
the character's normal abilities become unavailable;
the player may continue with another available party member if the encounter rules allow;
the character can only return through permitted revive effects or post-encounter recovery.
Historical documentation already established that 0 HP removes a character from active combat until revived.
Revive should be scarce enough that defeat remains meaningful.
Infinite or trivial revival would make failure irrelevant and should be avoided.
The game does not use permanent character death for normal gameplay.
recovery can occur through healing systems, checkpoints, items, or post-encounter rules.
This follows the Friction and Failure principle established in the Core Gameplay Loop: failure should encourage learning, adaptation, and retry rather than punitive loss.

Combat readability is critical. The player must be able to understand enemy intentions, character states, cooldowns, resources, elements, and reactions without depending on constant external explanation.
active character and available party members.
break, stagger, armor, or phase state when relevant.
When an elemental or special interaction occurs, the game should communicate the sequence clearly:
show the elements or powers involved;
play a readable visual and audio effect;
The player should not need to open an external wiki to understand why damage, control, resistance, or another combat condition changed.

No single communication channel should carry the entire burden. Critical attacks should remain readable even when color alone is insufficient.

This example uses existing characters from the historical documentation to demonstrate the intended combat logic. It is illustrative and does not lock the Vertical Slice roster or final character kits.
Suki iRonin. Cryo / Vigilante / Debuffer. Applies and strengthens negative states.
Juro Octophus. Chaos / Executioner. Consumes HP, generates tentacles, and gains offensive value from missing health.
Serverus Lazoi. Illumination / Theologian. Historical material links his kit to light/elemental amplification.
Hizuka Tamayo. Spectrum / Medic. Improves healing and converts part of that healing into shielding.
Prototype Guardian. High Cryo resistance, a heavily telegraphed high-damage attack, and medium physical resistance.
Suki's Cryo damage is inefficient because the Guardian's Cryo resistance is high. The player can continue attacking, but doing so would ignore the tools available in the party.
Suki applies a Cryo ability that also establishes a debuff. The immediate damage is limited, but the enemy is now prepared for a follow-up interaction.
Decision: sacrifice immediate damage to establish a favorable condition.
The player swaps to Juro and uses a Chaos ability. Historical design establishes Chaos as a power capable of reducing resistance associated with an elemental state.
Juro pays part of the cost with his own HP and generates a tentacle, creating a second decision layer: the team gains offensive value, but Juro becomes more vulnerable.
Decision: accept controlled risk in exchange for weakening the enemy.

The Guardian telegraphs a heavy attack. Juro is already exposed because of his HP cost. The player must decide whether to keep him active to exploit his missing-health bonuses, dodge and maintain the risk, or bring in protection.
Decision: determine how much risk the party can safely preserve.
The player brings in Hizuka and uses a healing action. Her documented Medical identity converts part of the healing into a shield.
Juro receives enough recovery to survive, but the player does not necessarily need to return him to full HP. The party preserves part of his missing-health identity while preventing a collapse.
Decision: stabilize the party without erasing the advantage created by controlled risk.
Serverus applies or refreshes an Illumination effect that strengthens the prepared elemental state, following the project's historical concept in which Illumination amplifies elemental magic.

The player returns to Suki during the vulnerability window and uses her main Cryo offensive ability. The attack now has substantially more impact than it did at the beginning of the encounter.
The Guardian enters low-HP range. Juro's Executioner identity can then gain additional value against a near-defeated target, giving the player another possible finishing route.
but that route would be slower and strategically shallow.
Juro weakens the enemy and accepts risk.
Juro can execute if the enemy reaches the appropriate threshold.
Victory comes not simply from higher statistics, but from understanding how four character identities can form one deliberate strategy.
